title: [Chapitre] VIII. Analysis situs (quatrième mouture) : notes manuscrites (26/06-04/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: the 1986 'Analysis situs' notes axiomatize a point-free theory of 'figures/regions' called 'magasins'. A magasin is a set M of regions with three relations: X ≤ Y (inclusion); Z ≪° X ('Z lies in the interior of X', a strict, well-inside type relation); and X |·| Y ('X and Y are essentially disjoint', i.e. their interiors do not meet). The general axioms are Mag 1–Mag 4 (p. 22), with a 'quasi-set-theoretic' variant Mag 3' (p. 24) and the set-theoretic models Magens 1–2 (p. 9).

The previous page showed one direction: X |·| Y implies {X,Y} has no common ≪°-lower bound. Otherwise some Z ≪° X, Z ≪° Y would give Z ≪° Z by Mag 3b, which Mag 3a forbids. The converse fails in general. Two distinct lines x, y in L have no common ≪°-minorant (lines have empty interior), yet they are not disjoint in the |·| sense.

This page therefore reverses the viewpoint. Take only (M, ≤, ≪°) and DEFINE (*) X |·| Y ⇔ {X,Y} has no lower bound in (M, ≪°). Then ask which axioms on ≤ and ≪° make (M, ≤, ≪°, |·|) a magasin.
- Mag 1 and Mag 2, rewritten with primes as conditions on ≤ and ≪°, are clear.
- Mag 3' becomes automatic, since (*) builds it in.
- Mag 4' follows from Mag 2' (insertion read as 'résulte de Mag 2'').

Proposition (stated without proof): magasins (M, ≤, ≪°) with |·| given by (*) are characterized by:
- Mag 1': ≤ and ≪° are order relations (≪° necessarily strict);
- Mag 2': the 'hexagon' compatibility condition of p. 22.

Grothendieck remarks this is 'formally as simple as the set-theoretic case': no Mag 4 needs to be added as on p. 24. He then records a hierarchy of increasingly special structures:
1. general magasins (≤, ≪°, |·|; Mag 1–4);
2. ⇐ magasins (≤, ≪°; Mag 1', Mag 2');
3. ⇐ quasi-set-theoretic magasins (Mag 1', 2', 3', p. 24);
4. ⇐ set-theoretic magasins (Magens 1, 2, p. 9).

He announces that magasins presented by (≤, |·|) alone, with other axioms, will also be needed, sitting between the general and the set-theoretic ones. The purpose is a combinatorial/tame-topological foundation in which regions of mixed dimension (lines, points, open regions) are handled without points. Next page: 'combinatorial maps' between magasins, e.g. molecules/atoms in Fig(L).
errors: The proposition is asserted without proof. Its content depends on the 'hexagon' axiom of p. 22, which is not reproduced here, so it cannot be checked from this page.
Calling ≪° a 'relation d'ordre' must mean a strict (irreflexive) order. The previous page uses Z ≪° Z as absurd (Mag 3a).

By the previous page's own example (two distinct lines), definition (*) does not recover the intended |·| in magasins containing interior-empty, lower-dimensional elements. So the (≤, ≪°)-magasins form a genuinely restricted class, not a presentation of all general magasins. Grothendieck acknowledges this through the hierarchy, but the term 'magasins' for the middle class is ambiguous.

ideas.what: Defining essential disjointness of regions as the absence of a common 'interior-part' lower bound: X |·| Y iff no Z with Z ≪° X and Z ≪° Y.
ideas.modern_name: Overlap/disjointness defined from a parthood or well-inside relation (mereology: O(x,y) ⇔ ∃z z≤x ∧ z≤y); external connection versus overlap in mereotopology (Region Connection Calculus, contact algebras)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Leśniewski / Tarski (mereology, geometry of solids 1929); Whitehead (1929); Clarke (1981); Randell–Cui–Cohn (RCC, 1992); de Vries (compingent algebras, 1962)
ideas.where_published: Only in the unpublished Analysis situs manuscripts (Montpellier, cote 156). Esquisse d'un programme §5–6 sketches 'tame topology' in general terms only.

ideas.what: Characterization of magasins presented by (≤, ≪°) alone through two axioms: both relations are orders, plus a 'hexagon' compatibility condition. The remaining axioms become automatic.
ideas.modern_name: Axiomatization of a point-free region structure with an inclusion and a well-inside relation (cf. proximity/contact algebras, way-below relation in continuous posets)
ideas.usually_credited_to: de Vries (1962); Scott (continuous lattices, 1972); Düntsch–Vakarelov, Bennett–Düntsch (contact algebras, 2000s)

ideas.what: Hierarchy of region structures: general ⇐ (≤, ≪°)-presented ⇐ quasi-set-theoretic ⇐ set-theoretic. Lower-dimensional strata (lines with empty interior) are explicitly accommodated.
ideas.modern_name: Hierarchy of mereotopological theories / point-free models of stratified (tame) spaces
ideas.usually_credited_to: mereotopology literature (Cohn, Varzi, Pratt-Hartmann); stratified tame topology (o-minimality: van den Dries)

missed.claim: Grothendieck is independently building a point-free mereotopology in 1986. It has inclusion, an interior/well-inside relation and a derived disjointness relation, closely parallel to Whitehead–Clarke connection calculus, de Vries compingent algebras and the later RCC/contact-algebra literature. Its distinctive twist is a deliberate focus on mixed-dimensional regions (lines, points) inside a tame-topology programme. To my knowledge the literature has not connected Grothendieck's 'topologie modérée' programme with mereotopology or contact algebras.
missed.quote: X |·| Y ⟺ {X,Y} non minoré dans M_≪° ... C'est formellement aussi simple que les cas ensemblistes !
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It could inform point-free foundations for o-minimal or stratified tame topology. Mereotopology mostly handles regular (full-dimensional) regions; these notes treat lower-dimensional figures as first-class.

missed.claim: Two items are left open on this page: the announced intermediate class of magasins presented by (≤, |·|) with 'other axioms', and a proof of the characterization proposition.
missed.quote: On sera amené aussi à considérer les magasins ≤, |·|, qui auront d'autres axiomes (qui se trouvent entre les magasins généraux et les ensemblistes...)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a small but concrete axiomatization question. It is accessible if the p. 22 hexagon axiom is recovered from the archive.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics itself is elementary order theory, similar to standard mereological definitions of overlap. The interest is historical: an unpublished, independent axiomatization of point-free region structures with lower-dimensional strata, apparently unconnected in the literature to mereotopology or contact algebras.
